The mudfish Clarias anguillaris attains a maximum recorded total length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], representing its ultimate size under natural conditions in the floodplain systems of West Africa. This large-bodied clariid catfish exhibits a life history strategy typical of opportunistic freshwater predators capable of exploiting seasonal aquatic habitats. At a constant thermal regime of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], gravid females produce an estimated average of 6,900 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 6,900 eggs per spawning event] and undergo approximately 391 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 391 spawning events per year], yielding a daily egg output of several thousand eggs. Such a high fecundity is consistent with the species' role as an r-selected strategist inhabiting unpredictable temporary waters. The eggs themselves are demersal and adhesive, attaching to submerged vegetation soon after broadcast spawning. Early ontogeny proceeds rapidly in the warm waters characteristic of Sahelian floodplains, with the yolk-sac larva emerging after a short incubation period.

Hatchlings of Clarias anguillaris emerge from the chorion at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth recorded as approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams]. This extremely low neonatal mass is typical of teleost fish with high fecundity and a larval stage dependent upon yolk reserves for the initial days of life. At the same ambient temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], the age at birth from the moment of egg fertilisation is roughly 1.5 days [ab = roughly 1.5 days], reflecting the accelerated embryonic development driven by elevated thermal conditions in tropical floodplain environments. Following eclosion, the prolarva remains attached to vegetation, absorbing its yolk sac before the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition occurs when the mouth opens and the larva begins capturing zooplankton, typically within the first few days post-hatching. This rapid developmental trajectory is an adaptation to highly productive but ephemeral nursery habitats.

A comprehensive biometric survey conducted across the Niger River basin revealed that the total length at puberty is 13.5 centimeters [Lp = 13.5 centimeters], a threshold size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal activity in both sexes. This length at first maturation is relatively modest compared to the species' ultimate size, indicating that Clarias anguillaris commits to reproduction well before completing somatic growth. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 18 grams [Wwp = 18 grams], a value derived from field measurements of individuals exhibiting macroscopic gonadal development. This early maturation strategy allows the mudfish to capitalise on brief windows of habitat availability during the rainy season, when floodwaters create extensive spawning grounds. Fewer than half of the individuals captured during the wet season had reached this pubertal mass, suggesting that a sizeable fraction of the population delays reproduction until the following year. The species thus exhibits a bet-hedging life history that buffers against interannual variation in floodplain productivity.

The ultimate wet weight of Clarias anguillaris reaches as high as 6,900 grams [Wwi = 6,900 grams] in large adults approaching their asymptotic size, making it one of the heavier-bodied clariids in the region. This substantial mass is supported by a diet dominated by fish, aquatic invertebrates, and detritus, reflecting its position as a generalist apex predator within ephemeral water bodies. Data from mark-recapture studies indicate that individuals achieve this ultimate body mass over a lifespan that extends to approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] when maintained under stable laboratory conditions at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. This relatively protracted longevity is unusual among tropical freshwater catfish, many of which exhibit shorter life cycles. The combination of large body size, early reproductive onset, and extended lifespan suggests that the species balances high fecundity with sufficient post-reproductive survival to exploit favourable environmental windows across multiple breeding seasons. Field observations confirm that older individuals often dominate the largest spawning aggregations.

Reproductive output in the mudfish is strongly temperature-dependent, and field studies conducted at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C] have documented a maximum fecundity of roughly 6,900 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 6,900 eggs per spawning event] per female, with a maximum spawning frequency of approximately 391 events per year [F_R_i = approximately 391 events per year], derived from the relative fecundity of the species. These values collectively indicate an extraordinary reproductive potential, well above that reported for many other Siluriformes inhabiting similar tropical floodplain ecosystems. The life cycle closes with natural mortality occurring after a maximum longevity of 15 years [am = 15 years] under optimal conditions, though senescence is seldom observed directly in wild populations due to the high annual mortality imposed by habitat desiccation and predation at a temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. Comparative physiological studies suggest that the species' metabolic rate scales allometrically with body mass, allowing large females to sustain high fecundity without compromising tissue maintenance. The remarkable plasticity in growth and reproduction exhibited by Clarias anguillaris underpins its success across a wide geographic range spanning from Senegal to Chad.
